argument: Building on his metaphysics of the will to life, Schopenhauer argues that human beings default into either restless striving punctuated by brief relief (mistaken for happiness) or boredom, anxiety, and depression when no goal is present -- and that pleasure itself is never a positive addition but merely a temporary subtraction of an underlying, ever-present suffering. Aesthetic absorption offers a fleeting, imperfect escape by stilling desire for a moment, but only the rare 'sage,' who recognizes the ultimate oneness of all suffering and wages an ascetic war on the will itself, achieves lasting escape. The episode closes by contrasting this with Nietzsche, who accepts the same premise of inescapable suffering but counsels embracing and being strengthened by it rather than fleeing it.
keyIdeas: As manifestations of the will to life, humans are locked in a default state of restless striving; achieving any given goal never produces lasting satisfaction because the will immediately generates a new object of desire, and people who habituate to this background suffering (like a war veteran tuning out chronic pain) mistake not noticing it for its absence.

Pleasure upon getting what you want is not a positive state added on top of a neutral baseline -- it is simply the temporary subtraction of the suffering that is our normal condition, revealed rather than created.

Ceaseless strivers distract themselves from suffering through constant pursuit, while the goal-less fall into boredom, anxiety, or depression because the will to life still drives them subconsciously with nowhere to direct itself.
Aesthetic absorption in beauty, art, or an immersive view offers a temporary escape because total presence in the moment halts the mind's habitual projection toward future wants.

The rare 'sage,' recognizing that all suffering is metaphysically one, achieves the only complete escape by waging an ascetic inner war against the will itself -- a solution Nietzsche, sharing the same premise of inexorable suffering, rejects in favor of embracing suffering as a resource that builds strength.

terms.def: The single underlying metaphysical force of which all individual things are manifestations, driving restless striving and interference with other manifestations of itself.
The rare person who, recognizing metaphysical monism, wages an internal war against the will to life and lives an ascetic existence as the pinnacle of Schopenhauer's ethics.
The view that everything in the universe is ultimately one thing, so that all suffering anywhere is, in a real sense, one's own suffering.
A lifestyle of renouncing sex, rich food, fame, and fortune, adopted by the sage as a rejection of the will's demands.

anchors: Schopenhauer thinks that because we’re all manifestations of this will to life, from the moment we come out of the womb, we’re in this constant state of restlessly striving for things.
Schopenhauer compares it to running through a sunny field. There’s sunlight all around you. But there’s a single dark cloud in the sky that’s hanging directly over your head.
It’s not that happiness has been added when you get the car, but that suffering has been subtracted.
Just because this suffering is the only life we’ve ever known, and we’ve learned to accept it and not allow it to make us miserable doesn’t mean that the suffering isn’t there.

You have the people that are going to ceaselessly strive and desire things for the rest of their life, and they’re just going to do their best to try to tune out the suffering along the way. And you have people that won’t have meaningful goals, and they’re all going to end up bored, anxious, or depressed.
We love it because it allows us, if only for a couple of minutes, to escape this state of constantly striving and desiring and reaching for things.
